questions.stem: In the sentence "The choir sang the hymn sweetly", the word *sweetly* modifies
questions.explanation: *Sweetly* answers the question "how did they sing?", so it modifies the verb *sang* and is therefore an adverb of manner. Words ending in -ly that answer how, when, where or to what extent almost always attach to the verb.

distractorRationale.a: To describe the choir you would need an adjective such as *sweet*: 'the sweet choir'
distractorRationale.b: To describe the hymn you would need 'a sweet hymn'
distractorRationale.d: Sentence adverbs such as *fortunately* or *obviously* modify a whole sentence, but *sweetly* points only at the action

questions.stem: Which word is used as an adjective in the sentence "The diligent student answered the difficult question confidently"?
questions.explanation: *Diligent* describes the noun *student*, and describing a noun is exactly what an adjective does. *Difficult* is also an adjective in this sentence, describing *question*, but it is not among the options.

distractorRationale.b: *Answered* is the finite verb of the sentence
distractorRationale.c: *Confidently* ends in -ly and tells how the student answered, so it is an adverb
distractorRationale.d: *Student* is the noun being described, not the describing word

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The second essay question was ______ than the first."
questions.explanation: Adjectives of three or more syllables form the comparative with *more*, not with -er, so *difficult* becomes *more difficult*. The word *than* in the sentence signals that a comparison between two items is being made, which calls for the comparative rather than the superlative degree.

distractorRationale.a: Adds -er to a three-syllable adjective, which English does not allow
distractorRationale.c: Uses the superlative, but *than* shows only two items are being compared
distractorRationale.d: *Very difficult* is the positive degree intensified; it cannot be followed by *than*

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Of the three prefects, Amina is by far the ______."
questions.explanation: Three items are being compared, and the superlative degree is used whenever more than two things are ranked. Because *responsible* has four syllables, the superlative is formed with *most*, giving *most responsible*. The definite article *the* before the blank is another clue that a superlative is expected.

distractorRationale.a: The comparative is for exactly two items, but there are three prefects here
distractorRationale.c: *Much* intensifies but does not compare, and it cannot follow *the*

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: The new Abuja road is more better than the old one.
The new Abuja road is more good than the old one.
The new Abuja road is better than the old one.
The new Abuja road is the most better than the old one.

questions.explanation: *Good* is an irregular adjective whose comparative is the single word *better*. Because *better* already carries the comparative meaning, adding *more* creates a double comparative, which is always an error.

distractorRationale.a: Double comparative: *more* and *better* both mark comparison
distractorRationale.b: Uses *more* with the positive form of an irregular adjective instead of the irregular comparative
distractorRationale.d: Mixes a superlative with a comparative structure using *than*

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The lorry driver negotiated the sharp bend very ______."
questions.explanation: The missing word tells us how the driver negotiated the bend, so it modifies the verb *negotiated* and must be an adverb: *carefully*. The intensifier *very* in front of the blank also points to an adverb or adjective rather than a noun.

distractorRationale.a: *Careful* is an adjective and would have to describe a noun, but there is no noun for it here
distractorRationale.c: *Carefulness* is an abstract noun and cannot follow *very*
distractorRationale.d: The comparative form would require a *than* clause, which the sentence does not have

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "When the results were announced, the children looked ______."
questions.explanation: Here *looked* is a linking verb meaning 'appeared', so the word after it describes the children, not the manner of looking. A word describing a noun is an adjective, so *happy* is correct. Compare "She looked at me happily", where *looked* is an action verb and the adverb is right.

distractorRationale.a: Would mean the children performed the act of looking in a happy manner, which is not the sense intended
distractorRationale.c: *Happiness* is a noun and would need a verb such as *showed* before it
distractorRationale.d: Adds a comparative to an adverb that does not belong in the sentence at all

questions.stem: An adverb can modify an adjective, as *extremely* does in the phrase *extremely hot afternoon*.
questions.explanation: True. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. In *extremely hot*, the adverb *extremely* tells us to what degree the afternoon was hot, so it modifies the adjective *hot*, which in turn modifies the noun *afternoon*.

questions.stem: You want to say that the number of mangoes you ate was no more than two. Which sentence expresses this exactly?
questions.explanation: *Only* restricts whatever immediately follows it, so it must sit directly in front of *two mangoes* to limit the quantity. Placing a modifier next to the word it limits is the general rule for keeping meaning precise.

distractorRationale.a: Placed before the verb, *only* suggests that eating was all you did with them — you did not sell or share them
distractorRationale.c: Placed before *I*, it means nobody else ate any mangoes
distractorRationale.d: Breaks the noun phrase and produces an ungrammatical sentence

questions.stem: Which of the following phrases places the adjectives in the natural English order?
questions.explanation: When several adjectives modify one noun, English fixes their order as opinion, then size, then age, shape, colour, origin and finally material. *Beautiful* is an opinion, *large* is a size and *wooden* is a material, so that is the sequence. The material adjective always sits closest to the noun.

distractorRationale.a: Puts the material adjective first, which sounds wrong to a native ear
distractorRationale.b: Puts size before opinion; opinion adjectives come first
